description: We are STEM students in grade 11. We enjoy creating projects, solving problems, doing research, and learning skills from each other. We are interested in technology, coding, astronomy, space exploration, analyzing data, and turning complex information into simple and engaging ideas, as well as NASA missions, especially those related to the Moon and Mars.
summary: This interactive website is aimed at children aged 12. Its main idea is to help children learn about and identify things left in space long ago through simplified explanations suitable for their age, with interactive games and an engaging approach.
details:
Project name: The Lunar Archive

What it does and how it works
The Lunar Archive is an interactive website that takes visitors on a trip to the Moon to find out what astronauts left behind. A talking robot welcomes the explorer inside a spaceship and introduces the idea that astronauts left more than footprints. Some objects finished their mission, some never worked, and some are still working. The visitor then watches a launch video and lands on the Moon, where a 360° panorama slowly rotates. A play button on the lunar lander opens the first object, Apollo 11. There, the visitor watches a short intro video and reads the mission in six short parts: the crew, the moonwalk, exploring the surface, the two-part Eagle spaceship, the EASEP science experiments, and what happened in the end. A summary window recaps it. At the end, the visitor plays a drag-and-drop puzzle to rebuild the lunar module. The puzzle has a progress bar, a success message, and a replay option.

Benefits

  • Learners explore the Moon instead of only reading about it.
  • The robot’s voice and short story parts help younger learners and those who don’t like long texts.
  • It runs in any browser with nothing to install.
  • Skip, back, and summary buttons let each visitor go at their own pace.

Intended impact
We want to spark curiosity about space exploration and show that Apollo 11 left scientific equipment and part of the Eagle on the Moon. The structure can grow with more objects, since the robot says “Let’s explore some of them!”

Tools, languages and software

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the pages, animations, story logic and puzzle.
  • Pannellum (a JavaScript library) for the 360° panorama.
  • Google Fonts (Black Ops One and Sniglet).
  • Audio files for the robot’s voice and the background music, video files for the launch and Apollo 11 intro, and PNG and JPEG images for the artwork.
  • Editors, image or video tools: [CapCut, Canva].

How it is creative

  • It treats Moon objects as an “archive” to explore, not a lesson to read.
  • A robot guide with its own voice leads the visitor.
  • It mixes video, a 360° panorama, a story, and a game in one trip.

What the team considered

  • Audience: learners who are curious about space and may be young.
  • Accuracy: the Apollo 11 facts, all from NASA resources.
  • Engagement: each part changes format so the visitor doesn’t get bored.
  • Control: every video and story can be skipped.
  • Access: it works in a browser.
  • Roles: We divided the tasks early, considering the shortage of the time.
